plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a labeled cross-sectional diagram of a Downs cell, the industrial electrolytic apparatus used to produce pure sodium metal from molten sodium chloride via the reaction 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g). The cell interior contains a bath of molten NaCl, with a cylindrical iron screen separating the electrode compartments; the cathode (−) occupies the outer annular region and the anode (+) projects upward from the bottom center, both connected to an external voltage source at the lower right. Liquid sodium metal, which is less dense than the molten salt, rises and collects in a side reservoir on the right, from which it drains through a labeled Na outlet; simultaneously, Cl2 gas produced at the anode rises through a central green-tinted collector tube and exits through a labeled Cl2 outlet at the upper right, while fresh NaCl is fed continuously through an inlet at the top. The iron screen physically segregates the two products — liquid sodium and gaseous chlorine — preventing their recombination and enabling continuous, separate collection of each. This figure demonstrates the Downs cell as the industrial-scale process for sodium production and explains why aqueous electrolysis cannot substitute for it, since H+ ions are more easily reduced than Na+ ions at any cathode in contact with water.

interactionPlan.concept: In a Downs cell, electrolysis of molten NaCl drives Cl⁻ to the central anode (oxidation to Cl₂ gas) and Na⁺ to the surrounding cathode (reduction to liquid Na), with an iron screen keeping the two products from recombining so each can be collected separately.
elements: Thick dark-gray outer cell casing drawn in cross-section (rectangular vessel with rounded inner cavity)
Pale lavender/blue body of molten NaCl filling the cell, with a horizontal blue liquid-surface line near the top
Central orange anode (+) column rising from the bottom center with a flared orange head near the top of the column
Two dark blue-gray cathode (−) bars in the outer annular region, left and right of the screen, connected to horizontal feedthrough bars passing through the casing wall
Cylindrical iron screen drawn as a curved cross-hatched mesh barrier surrounding the anode region
Black funnel/hood above the anode that narrows into the vertical Cl₂ collector tube
Pale green vertical Cl₂ collector tube bending right at the top into a horizontal duct
Small pale-green gas bubbles rising from the anode head up through the funnel into the tube
Black upward arrow inside the collector tube indicating gas flow
Arrow and label 'Cl₂ outlet' at upper right
Inlet pipe at the top of the cell with a small vertical stem, labeled 'Inlet for NaCl' with leader line to the right
Right-side sodium riser channel and pale pink flask-shaped reservoir holding liquid Na, labeled 'Liquid Na metal'
Pale pink liquid sodium layer resting above the molten salt level in the reservoir and a thin pink band inside the cell marking the sodium layer
Downspout from the reservoir to the right with arrow, labeled 'Na outlet'
Gray 'Voltage source' box at lower right with thick black wires running to the anode stem and to the right-hand cathode feedthrough
Label with leader line: 'Molten NaCl' on the left
Label with leader line: 'Iron screen' on the left
Labels with leader lines at the bottom: 'Cathode (−)' and 'Anode (+)'
Overlay panel (appears on interaction) showing the half-reaction equations: 2Cl⁻(l) → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻ and 2Na⁺(l) + 2e⁻ → 2Na(l), plus the overall 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl₂(g)
Animated ion markers: green Cl⁻ circles and purple Na⁺ circles drifting through the melt

interactions.label: Run electrolysis
interactions.teaches: Charge carriers move continuously: Cl⁻ migrates inward to the anode and bubbles off as Cl₂ that escapes up the collector tube, while Na⁺ migrates outward to the cathode and the resulting liquid Na floats up and drains to the Na outlet.
Which half-reaction happens where — clicking the anode or the cathode highlights that compartment and displays its balanced half-equation with electron flow direction.
interactions.teachesDetail: Anode = oxidation of chloride; cathode = reduction of sodium ion.

interactions.label: Iron screen
interactions.teaches: Without the screen, rising Na and Cl₂ meet and recombine violently; the screen is what makes separate, safe collection of the two products possible.

demo_steps.title: The cell at rest
demo_steps.narration: A steel vessel holds molten NaCl above 800 °C. A central graphite anode sits inside a cylindrical iron screen; the ring-shaped cathode surrounds it. No current flows yet, so the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions drift randomly.

demo_steps.title: Switch on the voltage source
demo_steps.narration: With the external supply connected, ions stop drifting and start migrating: green Cl⁻ moves inward to the positive anode, purple Na⁺ moves outward to the negative cathode.

demo_steps.title: Oxidation at the anode
demo_steps.narration: Click the orange anode: each pair of chloride ions gives up electrons, 2Cl⁻(l) → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻. Bubbles collect in the hood and rise through the green tube to the Cl₂ outlet.

demo_steps.title: Reduction at the cathode
demo_steps.narration: Click the outer cathode bars: Na⁺(l) + e⁻ → Na(l). Molten sodium is less dense than the salt bath, so it floats to the top, fills the side reservoir, and drains out the Na outlet.

demo_steps.title: Why the iron screen matters
demo_steps.narration: Remove the screen and the rising sodium meets the chlorine bubbles — the products recombine back into NaCl (and dangerously so). The screen keeps the two half-cell products physically apart, which is what makes the process continuous and useful.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Electrolysis only pays off industrially if the two products are kept apart — the Downs cell's geometry (central anode, surrounding cathode, iron screen, buoyant liquid Na, rising Cl₂ gas) is engineered entirely around separating sodium from chlorine the instant they form.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Centered cross-sectional schematic on white. Thick dark-gray double-walled vessel outline forms a squarish cell with a rounded inner cavity; interior filled pale lavender-blue (molten NaCl) with a horizontal medium-blue line marking the melt surface near the top. From the bottom center an orange column (anode, +) rises to about mid-height and ends in a wider orange flared head. A black funnel/hood sits just above that head and narrows into a pale yellow-green vertical tube that exits the top of the cell, bends right, and runs horizontally to a black arrow labeled 'Cl₂ outlet' at the upper right. Small pale green bubble dots drift from the anode head up into the funnel and tube; a long black arrow inside the tube shows gas direction. A curved cross-hatched mesh (iron screen) arcs around the anode region, drawn as a fine grid with slightly bowed top and bottom edges. Two dark slate-blue vertical bars flank the screen outside it (cathode, −), each joined to horizontal feedthrough bars that pierce the casing left and right. On the right, a channel leads up to a pale-pink flask/reservoir labeled 'Liquid Na metal', with a pink downspout exiting right to an arrow labeled 'Na outlet'; a thin pink band inside the cell shows the sodium layer floating on the melt. A small vertical stem on the cell lid is labeled 'Inlet for NaCl' by a leader line to the right. Lower right holds a gray 'Voltage source' box with thick black wires: one to the anode stem, one to the right cathode feedthrough. Left-side leader labels: 'Molten NaCl' and 'Iron screen'. Bottom leader labels: 'Cathode (−)' and 'Anode (+)'. Color coding for interaction: Cl⁻/Cl₂ in green, Na⁺/Na in pink-purple, anode highlight orange, cathode highlight blue. Half-reaction text appears in a light callout panel near the clicked electrode.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotesExtra: Animation should move ion markers along short radial paths (inward green, outward purple), spawn bubbles at the anode head, and gradually raise the pink level in the side reservoir with a small trickle at the Na outlet.

authoredContext:
The most important method for the production of sodium is the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride; the set-up is a Downs cell , shown in . The reaction involved in this process is:

Separation of the molten sodium and chlorine prevents recombination. The liquid sodium, which is less dense than molten sodium chloride, floats to the surface and flows into a collector. The gaseous chlorine goes to storage tanks. Chlorine is also a valuable product.

Pure sodium metal is isolated by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride using a Downs cell. It is not possible to isolate sodium by electrolysis of aqueous solutions of sodium salts because hydrogen ions are more easily reduced than are sodium ions; as a result, hydrogen gas forms at the cathode instead of the desired sodium metal. The high temperature required to melt NaCl means that liquid sodium metal forms.

A diagram is shown. At the center of the diagram is a T-shaped structure labeled, “Anode ( positive sign ),” that is on a mesh-like background labeled, “Iron screen.” The anode is connected to a box labeled, “Voltage source,” by a line, and the voltage source is connected to one of two L-shaped structures that surround the anode. They are labeled, “Cathode ( negative sign ).” Above the cathode on the right side of the diagram is a tube connected to a collection chamber labeled, “N a metal,” that has a lower outlet labeled, “N a outlet.” Surrounding all of these components is a blue background labeled, “Molten N a C l,” and a series of tubes that form a square outside the diagram. They have an opening in the upper right corner labeled, “Inlet for N a C l.” At the top of the diagram is a large tube with an upward-facing arrow drawn on it. The tube turns right, has a right-facing arrow on it, and is labeled, “C l subscript 2 outlet.”

attempts.html:
Downs cell — electrolysis of molten NaCl

Click the orange anode or the blue cathode bars in the figure; hover any part for a label. Green = Cl⁻/Cl₂, purple-pink = Na⁺/Na.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Default (step-0) state shows a scattering of green Cl⁻ and purple Na⁺ dots throughout the melt, while the source shows only a stream of pale yellow-green Cl₂ bubbles rising from the anode hood into the collector tube — the characteristic bubble plume is absent at rest and the extra ion dots change the at-a-glance look.

The sodium reservoir is drawn as a rounded bulb on a stem; in the source it is a distinctly flask/funnel-shaped vessel with a narrow neck at top widening downward, with the pink liquid level line clearly inside it.

Anode head in the source is a wide flat-topped block whose width roughly matches the screen interior and whose stem exits through the bottom wall of the cell; the generated anode head is narrower and the stem is thinner relative to the cell, making the central electrode less prominent.

The source's left/right blue-gray cathode feed-through bars are longer and symmetric, and the source's hood lines meet the screen top exactly at its rim; in the generated version the hood lines and screen rim meet slightly off, leaving small gaps at the funnel/screen junction.
evaluation.notes: A well-composed, clearly recognizable Downs-cell reproduction with correct labels, colors and chemistry, plus a genuinely useful 5-step demo, toggles and electrode half-reaction popups; main weaknesses are the missing Cl₂ bubble plume in the default resting state (replaced by scattered ion dots) and a few shape/proportion deviations in the sodium flask and anode.

feedback.rationale: The concept, interaction structure, and labels are correct; remaining issues are concrete rendering details (default-state Cl₂ bubble plume, flask/anode shapes, hood-screen junction) that belong to implementation refinement.

discrepancies: Right-hand sodium reservoir is simplified and under-scaled: the source shows a tall flask with a distinct narrow neck and a wide conical body sitting well above the cell rim; the generated bulb is short and squat, so the 'Liquid Na metal' vessel reads less clearly.

The Cl₂ hood/collector geometry is slightly off: the source funnel tapers gradually from the wide skirt over the anode up into a narrow riser, while the generated hood is a near-parallel green column with an abrupt junction and a thicker elbow stroke.

The pink molten-sodium layer is rendered as a single straight bar across the melt; in the source it appears as short pink segments at the melt/screen interface on either side, and the melt surface line placement differs slightly.
Label text is rendered at roughly 12 px effective size after down-scaling — noticeably smaller and lighter than the source's prominent annotation type, weakening the label hierarchy.

Added elements not in the source (colored Na⁺/Cl⁻ ion dots, yellow electron dashes on the wires, an overlay callout box in the upper left) appear in later steps and can crowd the top-left of the drawing, though they are opt-in.
evaluation.notes: A close, well-composed reproduction of the Downs cell with correct colors, all source labels, and an unusually rich and pedagogically sound interaction set (5-step player, run/ions/screen toggles, electrode half-reaction highlights); weaknesses are small-scale geometry simplifications (sodium flask, hood taper, pink Na layer) and slightly undersized annotation text.
action_items: Increase annotation font size (≈17–18 px in the 750×620 viewBox) and bold the primary part labels so the hierarchy matches the source at inline scale.
Redraw the sodium reservoir as a taller narrow-neck flask with a conical body matching the source silhouette, and lengthen/taper the Cl₂ hood into a narrower riser.
Replace the single pink bar with the source's segmented sodium layer at the melt/screen interface, and check the melt surface line height against the source.
Reposition the step callout box so it never overlaps the 'Molten NaCl' label or the cell casing when steps 3–5 are active.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interaction structure are sound (concept 5, no failure modes); remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes—flask/hood geometry, pink layer segmentation, font sizing, and callout placement.

interactions.label: Run electrolysis
interactions.teaches: Charge carriers move continuously: Cl⁻ migrates inward to the anode and bubbles off as Cl₂ that escapes up the collector tube, while Na⁺ migrates outward to the cathode and the resulting liquid Na floats up and drains to the Na outlet.
Which half-reaction happens where — clicking the anode or the cathode highlights that compartment and displays its balanced half-equation with electron flow direction.
interactions.teachesDetail: Anode = oxidation of chloride; cathode = reduction of sodium ion.

interactions.label: Iron screen
interactions.teaches: Without the screen, rising Na and Cl₂ meet and recombine violently; the screen is what makes separate, safe collection of the two products possible.

demo_steps.title: The cell at rest
demo_steps.narration: A steel vessel holds molten NaCl above 800 °C. A central graphite anode sits inside a cylindrical iron screen; the ring-shaped cathode surrounds it. No current flows yet, so the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions drift randomly.

demo_steps.title: Switch on the voltage source
demo_steps.narration: With the external supply connected, ions stop drifting and start migrating: green Cl⁻ moves inward to the positive anode, purple Na⁺ moves outward to the negative cathode.

demo_steps.title: Oxidation at the anode
demo_steps.narration: Click the orange anode: each pair of chloride ions gives up electrons, 2Cl⁻(l) → Cl₂(g) + 2e⁻. Bubbles collect in the hood and rise through the green tube to the Cl₂ outlet.

demo_steps.title: Reduction at the cathode
demo_steps.narration: Click the outer cathode bars: Na⁺(l) + e⁻ → Na(l). Molten sodium is less dense than the salt bath, so it floats to the top, fills the side reservoir, and drains out the Na outlet.

demo_steps.title: Why the iron screen matters
demo_steps.narration: Remove the screen and the rising sodium meets the chlorine bubbles — the products recombine back into NaCl (and dangerously so). The screen keeps the two half-cell products physically apart, which is what makes the process continuous and useful.

plan.keyInsight: Electrolysis only pays off industrially if the two products are kept apart — the Downs cell's geometry (central anode, surrounding cathode, iron screen, buoyant liquid Na, rising Cl₂ gas) is engineered entirely around separating sodium from chlorine the instant they form.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Centered cross-sectional schematic on white. Thick dark-gray double-walled vessel outline forms a squarish cell with a rounded inner cavity; interior filled pale lavender-blue (molten NaCl) with a horizontal medium-blue line marking the melt surface near the top. From the bottom center an orange column (anode, +) rises to about mid-height and ends in a wider orange flared head. A black funnel/hood sits just above that head and narrows into a pale yellow-green vertical tube that exits the top of the cell, bends right, and runs horizontally to a black arrow labeled 'Cl₂ outlet' at the upper right. Small pale green bubble dots drift from the anode head up into the funnel and tube; a long black arrow inside the tube shows gas direction. A curved cross-hatched mesh (iron screen) arcs around the anode region, drawn as a fine grid with slightly bowed top and bottom edges. Two dark slate-blue vertical bars flank the screen outside it (cathode, −), each joined to horizontal feedthrough bars that pierce the casing left and right. On the right, a channel leads up to a pale-pink flask/reservoir labeled 'Liquid Na metal', with a pink downspout exiting right to an arrow labeled 'Na outlet'; a thin pink band inside the cell shows the sodium layer floating on the melt. A small vertical stem on the cell lid is labeled 'Inlet for NaCl' by a leader line to the right. Lower right holds a gray 'Voltage source' box with thick black wires: one to the anode stem, one to the right cathode feedthrough. Left-side leader labels: 'Molten NaCl' and 'Iron screen'. Bottom leader labels: 'Cathode (−)' and 'Anode (+)'. Color coding for interaction: Cl⁻/Cl₂ in green, Na⁺/Na in pink-purple, anode highlight orange, cathode highlight blue. Half-reaction text appears in a light callout panel near the clicked electrode.

discrepancies: The chlorine collector is drawn as a broad tapering green cone that starts very wide at the melt surface (≈60 px) and narrows upward; in the source the green pipe is a narrow constant-width riser and the flared collecting hood below the surface is drawn only as black outline lines, so the generated version reads as a large green funnel that dominates the cell interior.

The green riser bends right at a lower height and the elbow is much tighter/shorter than in the source, where the tube rises well above the cell before turning, making the top-left composition noticeably more compressed.
The voltage-source box is smaller relative to the cell than in the source and its wiring meets the cell lower/closer to the bottom, slightly changing the circuit layout proportions.

The iron-screen barrel mesh is coarser (fewer/straighter grid lines) and the sodium layer is reduced to two short pink bars, so the pink sodium surface layer inside the cell is less visible than in the source.

The side sodium riser/flask assembly sits slightly higher and closer to the vessel wall than in the source, and the horizontal pink duct penetrates the casing at a different height than the pink layer it drains.
evaluation.notes: A well-executed, clearly recognizable Downs-cell reproduction with all source labels present and correctly placed, backed by a genuinely pedagogical 5-step demo with working toggles, electrode half-reaction callouts and ion animation; main weaknesses are the over-flared green chlorine cone/hood and slightly compressed riser geometry versus the source.
action_items: Redraw the chlorine collector as a narrow constant-width green pipe with the flared hood rendered as black outline lines only (as in the source), and raise the elbow so the tube rises higher before turning right.
Enlarge the voltage-source box and route the cathode wire from the side feedthrough as in the source so the external circuit proportions match.
Increase mesh density on the iron-screen barrel and extend/darken the pink sodium layer bars so the floating Na layer aligns with the side riser inlet.
Slightly reduce the vertical extent of the anode stem below the cell so its proportion relative to the vessel matches the source.
